text: It is because of Yahweh’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his compassion doesn’t fail. They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.
reflection: Jeremiah writes this in the middle of a book about a burned city. He is not describing a good week; he is describing what held when everything else did not. The mercy is new every morning, which means yesterday's supply was never meant to cover today.
question: What are you carrying this morning that yesterday's strength cannot carry?
prayer: Lord, your mercies are new this morning. I need today's, not yesterday's.
practice: Before you open anything else on your phone, name one mercy from yesterday out loud.

text: Don’t you be afraid, for I am with you. Don’t be dismayed, for I am your God. I will strengthen you. Yes, I will help you. Yes, I will uphold you with the right hand of my righteousness.
reflection: Four promises follow the command, and not one of them is that the situation will change. God's answer to fear here is his own presence and his own grip — not a guarantee about the outcome.
question: What would you do this week if you actually believed you would be held through it?
prayer: God, I am afraid of a specific thing. Be with me in it, not only after it.
practice: Write the thing you are afraid of on one line. Put this verse under it.

text: I will lift up my eyes to the hills. Where does my help come from? My help comes from Yahweh, who made heaven and earth.
reflection: This is a song for people on a journey, sung by pilgrims a long way from home. The question is asked honestly before it is answered, which is the difference between faith and pretending.
question: Where have you been looking for help that cannot actually give it?
prayer: Lord, I have been asking the wrong sources. My help comes from you.
practice: Ask one person for the practical help you have been too proud to ask for.

text: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”
reflection: Jesus does not offer an empty shoulder; he offers a different yoke. The rest on offer is not the end of work — it is the end of carrying it alone, and for the wrong master.
question: Whose approval are you actually working for?
prayer: Jesus, I am tired in a way sleep does not fix. Teach me your pace.
practice: Choose one thing today you will leave undone, on purpose, without apologising for it.

text: Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.
reflection: Not leaning on your own understanding is not the same as switching your mind off. It is refusing to make your own read of a situation the final word when God has said something clearer.
question: Which decision are you making entirely on your own reading of it?
prayer: God, I have been sure of things I cannot actually see. Straighten this path.
practice: Take the decision you are turning over and tell it to God before you tell it to anyone else.

text: In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.
reflection: Paul writes this from prison, which is worth remembering before treating it as advice from someone whose life went well. The instruction is not to feel differently; it is to move the anxiety somewhere — into a specific request, with thanks attached.
question: What have you been rehearsing in your head instead of asking for?
prayer: Father, here is the request I keep rehearsing. I am handing it over, with thanks.
practice: Say the worry as an actual sentence to God, ending with one thing you are grateful for.

text: And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord, and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance; for you serve the Lord Christ.
reflection: This was first written to slaves, by a man who knew exactly what he was asking. It does not say the work is fair, or that the employer deserves it. It relocates who the work is finally for.
question: What would change in the next eight hours if the audience were God?
prayer: Lord, this job is hard and often unseen. Receive it as service to you.
practice: Do the part of your job nobody checks as carefully as the part they do.

text: But godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into the world, and we certainly can’t carry anything out. But having food and clothing, we will be content with that.
reflection: Contentment here is called gain, not sacrifice. Paul is not asking for a lower standard of living; he is pointing out that a life spent chasing the next amount never arrives, whatever the amount turns out to be.
question: What figure have you decided will finally be enough — and did the last one hold?
prayer: God, teach me the difference between what I need and what I am afraid of not having.
practice: Write down what you sent home or spent this month, and thank God for one line of it.

text: Let us not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season, if we don’t give up.
reflection: The warning is not against doing bad; it is against getting tired of doing good. Most people who stop did not decide to stop — they simply ran out of season before the harvest arrived.
question: What good thing are you close to quietly giving up on?
prayer: Lord, I am tired of doing the right thing with nothing to show for it. Hold me to it.
practice: Do the unrewarded good thing one more time today, without mentioning it.

text: For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing, will be able to separate us from God’s love, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
reflection: Paul lists everything he can think of and then closes the gap with a catch-all, because he knows the reader will try to think of one more. Distance is on the list. So is the future.
question: Which item on that list have you privately decided is the exception in your case?
prayer: Jesus, I have been living as though your love could run out on me. It cannot.
practice: Name the thing you fear has disqualified you, and read the list again.

text: bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.
reflection: Paul assumes the complaint is real. He does not ask anyone to decide they were not wronged — he asks them to forgive on the same terms they were forgiven, which were not terms the offender had earned.
question: Who are you waiting to deserve your forgiveness first?
prayer: Jesus, you forgave me before I made it right. Give me the will to do the same.
practice: Send one message you have been withholding out of principle.

text: Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations, knowing that the testing of your faith produces endurance. Let endurance have its perfect work, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.
reflection: James says count, not feel. It is an act of accounting — deciding what this hard thing is actually producing — rather than a demand to be cheerful about it.
question: What has this present difficulty already built in you that comfort never did?
prayer: God, I will not pretend this is good. Do the work in me that only this can do.
practice: Tell one trusted person what the hard season is teaching you, without minimising it.

text: Where could I go from your Spirit? Or where could I flee from your presence? If I ascend up into heaven, you are there. If I make my bed in Sheol, behold, you are there! If I take the wings of the dawn, and settle in the uttermost parts of the sea; Even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me.
reflection: David is imagining the furthest place he can picture and finding God already there. For anyone working a long flight away from the people they love, this is not poetry — it is the one address that did not change.
question: What have you assumed God is less present in because it is far from home?
prayer: Lord, you are as near here as you are where my family sleeps tonight.
practice: Pray for someone at home by name, at the hour they will be waking up.

text: He has said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Most gladly therefore I will rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest on me.
reflection: Paul asked three times for the thing to be removed and was told no, with a reason. The answer he got was not a smaller problem but a larger supply — and he came to prefer it.
question: What weakness have you been hiding that God intends to work through rather than remove?
prayer: Jesus, I have asked you to take this away. If it stays, be strong in it.
practice: Admit one limitation out loud to someone instead of working around it alone.

text: He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?
reflection: Micah's audience were offering God a great deal of religion. His answer strips it back to three things, all of which are done on ordinary days, in front of people who cannot repay you.
question: Which of the three — justice, mercy, humility — is the one you are avoiding?
prayer: God, I would rather give you religion than change. Make me just, merciful and small.
practice: Pick the one you avoid, and do it once today where nobody will know.
